LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Breathe, Brave, Try Again & I Can Do It — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson turns courage from a personality into a ladder: four rungs any child can climb the next time something feels too big.

What is this?

Breathe, brave, try again and I can do it are the four rungs of the courage ladder: a breath to steady the body, a brave thought to steady the mind, one more try to steady the habit and the little sentence that holds it all up.

What does it mean?

Big feelings shrink when the body calms first — that is why breathe comes BEFORE brave. Children who learn the order stop waiting to feel brave and discover that brave is something you DO, one breath at a time.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: the breath comes FIRST (in like a flower, out like a candle); brave is a thought you THINK, not a feeling you wait for; and try again is the rung you may climb as many times as you like.

Why this matters

This ladder is the first calm-down tool of the class, and it is reused by every later card — the pause, the count to ten, the reset. Learning it early means the harder moments later have somewhere to stand.

What it teaches

Self-regulation (the breath), courage as process, growth mindset (try again is the plantable phrase), and self-talk — the sentence I can do it is the first one children learn to say to themselves.

Words to learn

breathebravetry againI can do itbrave breathsteadycourage

Say this to your child

“"When something feels too big, we do not have to be the bravest person in the world — we just have to climb the ladder. Step one: breathe. In like you are smelling a flower, out like you are blowing a candle — do it twice. Step two: think brave — what would the brave version try? Step three: try again — one more go, wobbles allowed. Step four, the best one: say it, small and strong — I can do it. Because you can. And if the first try wobbles? The ladder is still there. It never runs out."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is the courage ladder — four steps up a wobbly moment."
  2. Climb it slowly: hands at the chest for BREATHE (in like a flower, out like a candle), fists up for BE BRAVE, forward lean for TRY AGAIN, fist up small and certain for I CAN DO IT.
  3. Pick one real wobbly thing — the big slide, a new food, the dark hallway — and climb the ladder out loud together.
  4. Tell the story of something YOU found scary and climbed: grown-up honesty is the best poster.
  5. Close with the game below and the takeaway: "brave is not a feeling you wait for — it is four steps you take."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels climb the ladder: Breathe, a boy with hands folded at his chest mid-breath; Be Brave, a girl in a little cape with her fist raised; Try Again, a determined boy with a raised fist; and I Can Do It, a confident girl with a small fist up — the four steps exactly as your child will climb them.

Ask your child

"What comes first — the breath or the brave?" "What does brave look like on this card?" "How many times may we try again?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Flower breath, candle breath!" "I can do it!" (the whole point) or the honest one: "I was scared and I did it anyway."

Out in the real world

Wobbly moments queue up daily: the tall slide, the swimming step, the new food touching the old food, the goodbye at preschool’s door. Climb the ladder at each one — quietly, quickly — and by the tenth climb your child starts it without you.

Try it together

Ladder Tag for Toys: line up three stuffed animals at the "too big slide" (a chair with a cushion). Each animal climbs the ladder out loud — breathe, brave, try again, I can do it — and takes the slide. Your child voices all three: shy voice, shaky voice, then the triumphant one. The third animal always makes it look easy.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is step one of the ladder? What do we say at the top? Does the ladder run out?" Breathe, I can do it, never — three answers and the ladder is theirs to climb.

Parent tips

Say the ladder with your child, never AT them — "let us climb it together" beats "just be brave" every single time. And celebrate the climb, not the landing: a child who breathed, thought brave and tried again SUCCEEDED, whatever the slide did.

This lesson pairs with the Breathe, Brave, Try Again & I Can Do It flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).
